1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Models.}
8	We evaluate seven models spanning five architecture families and diverse attention configurations:
9	\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA 7:1, 28 layers $\times$ 4 KV heads = 112),
10	\textbf{Qwen2.5-14B} (GQA 5:1, 48 $\times$ 8 = 384),
11	\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (GQA 8:1, 48 $\times$ 4 = 192),
12	\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256),
13	\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256, sliding window attention),
14	\textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (GQA 2:1, 42 $\times$ 8 = 336, \texttt{head\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping),
15	and \textbf{Pythia-1.4B} (MHA 1:1, 24 $\times$ 16 = 384).
16	This selection spans GQA ratios from 1:1 (MHA) to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, softcapped, and multi-head attention.
17	
18	\paragraph{Evaluation.}
19	We report perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.
20	For downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.
21	
22	\paragraph{Profiling.}
23	Per-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.
24	All results use high-resolution profiling (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens from WikiText-2 train); Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} compares against standard-resolution profiling (16 seq $\times$ 512 tok).
25	
26	\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}
27	The default target is 4$\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).
28	The cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \S\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen-7B and Qwen-14B, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2 and Pythia).
29	
30	\paragraph{Baselines.}
31	We compare against:
32	(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;
33	(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\cite{zuo2026ratequant});
34	(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;
35	(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\pm$std and median);
36	and (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.
37	
38	\subsection{Main Results}
39	\label{sec:main_results}
40	
41	\begin{table}[t]
42	\centering
43	\small
44	\caption{PPL ($\downarrow$) on WikiText-2 at 4$\times$ compression. Unconstrained failure: catastrophic on Qwen-7B ($3.3\times$ bf16), severe on Pythia ($1.9\times$), moderate on Gemma-2 ($1.5\times$), mild on remaining incl.\ Qwen-14B (${\sim}1.1\times$). Greedy and MCKP produce identical unconstrained allocations on 5/7 models. Best constrained result per model in \textbf{bold}. $^\ddagger$Best $k$ from ablation ($k{=}4$). $^*$BOS-corrected.}
45	\label{tab:main_results}
46	\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
47	\toprule
48	Model & Baseline & Uniform & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Unconstrained} & Ours \\
49	\cmidrule(lr){4-5}
50	 & (bf16) & (4-bit) & Greedy & MCKP & (Constr.) \\
51	\midrule
52	Qwen2.5-7B      & 9.81  & 15.45 & 32.45 & 36.92 & \textbf{10.91} \\
53	Qwen2.5-14B     & 6.87  & 7.20  & 7.69  & 7.69  & 7.22 \\
54	Yi-1.5-9B       & 7.02  & 7.22  & 7.56  & 7.56  & 7.22 \\
55	Llama-3.1-8B    & 8.09  & 8.47  & 8.63  & 8.63  & \textbf{8.45} \\
56	Mistral-7B-v0.3 & 7.04  & 7.13  & 7.57  & 7.60  & 7.16$^\ddagger$ \\
57	Gemma-2-9B$^*$  & 6.03  & 6.17  & 8.85  & 8.85  & 6.20 \\
58	Pythia-1.4B     & 16.49 & 24.29 & 31.54 & 31.54 & 24.45 \\
59	\bottomrule
60	\end{tabular}
61	\end{table}
62	
63	On Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 10.91 PPL, a 29.4\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45).
64	Without the constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure from excessive 2-bit assignments compounding across layers.
65	Across 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\pm$0.06 with 90.2\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.
66	
67	On Llama-3.1-8B, the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47, $\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
68	Hires profiling reveals concentration $0.57$ (comparable to Qwen's $0.61$) but a spike pattern ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) dominated by a single head (L2H5), leaving no cross-bitwidth gradient to exploit.
69	
70	On Yi-1.5-9B, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) matches uniform (7.22); despite the highest concentration tested (0.71), sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier (L4H3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern with no cross-bitwidth gradient.
71	On Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\%); near-zero sensitivity differences and sliding-window attention may both contribute.
72	
73	On Gemma-2-9B$^*$ (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 6.20 PPL vs.\ uniform 6.17 ($+$0.4\%).
74	Despite flat sensitivity (concentration 0.23), unconstrained MCKP degrades to 8.85 ($1.47\times$ bf16) from 31.5\% 2-bit over-allocation; the constraint reduces this to 8 heads, confirming universal over-allocation prevention.
75	
76	Unconstrained failure severity tracks heterogeneity shape: \emph{catastrophic} on Qwen-7B ($3.3\times$ bf16, 60\% heads at 2-bit), \emph{severe} on Pythia ($1.9\times$), \emph{moderate} on Gemma-2 ($1.47\times$), and \emph{mild} on remaining models (${\sim}1.07$--$1.12\times$) including Qwen-14B ($1.12\times$, 20\% 2-bit)---the within-family contrast directly reflects shape (spread vs.\ flat).
77	See Appendix~\ref{sec:allocation_appendix} (allocation visualization) and Appendix~\ref{sec:budget_sweep} (budget sweep) for additional detail.
78	
79	MCKP consistently outperforms random L0-constrained allocation and naive positional baselines across all three tested models (median gap 5--16\%; Table~\ref{tab:heuristic} in Appendix~\ref{sec:heuristic_appendix}).
80	
81	\paragraph{Comparison with KIVI.}
82	KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi} uses asymmetric per-channel quantization with per-token scaling, applied uniformly across all heads.
83	At 4-bit ($r{=}0$), KIVI achieves near-lossless PPL (9.91 on Qwen, 8.14 on Llama vs.\ 9.81/8.09 bf16), while our symmetric scheme yields 15.45 and 8.47---a gap from the quantization method, not allocation.
84	However, KIVI cannot exploit head-level heterogeneity: on Qwen (spread), constrained MCKP reduces symmetric 4-bit from 15.45 to 10.91 ($-$4.54 PPL) by reallocating bits across heads, a degree of freedom unavailable to uniform-precision methods; on Llama (spike), the gain is negligible ($-$0.02).
85	At 2-bit ($r{=}0$), KIVI degrades further (13.34 on Qwen, 10.08 on Llama) as sensitive heads receive the same precision as insensitive ones.
86	The two approaches are orthogonal and composable: KIVI selects the per-channel scheme, our method selects the per-head bit-width.
87	
88	\subsection{Downstream Evaluation}
89	\label{sec:downstream}
90	
91	\begin{table}[t]
92	\centering
93	\small
94	\caption{0-shot accuracy change (Ours $-$ Uniform, pts) at 4$\times$ compression. Qwen shows large gains; the remaining models show small degradations or neutrality, tracking PPL results.}
95	\label{tab:downstream}
96	\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
97	\toprule
98	Model & ARC-C & HS & PIQA & WG & Avg \\
99	\midrule
100	Qwen2.5-7B        & $+$3.2 & $+$4.0 & $+$1.3 & $+$2.0 & $+$2.6 \\
101	Yi-1.5-9B        & $-$3.2 & $-$0.6 & $-$0.3 & $+$1.3 & $-$0.8 \\
102	Llama-3.1-8B     & $-$2.7 & $-$0.1 & $-$0.7 & $-$0.2 & $-$1.0 \\
103	Mistral-7B       & $-$1.2 & $-$0.2 & $+$0.4 & $-$1.0 & $-$0.5 \\
104	Gemma-2-9B       & $-$0.2 & $+$0.3 & $-$0.1 & $+$0.8 & $+$0.1 \\
105	\bottomrule
106	\end{tabular}
107	\end{table}
108	
109	On Qwen, constrained MCKP improves average 0-shot accuracy by 2.6 pts over uniform (0.686 vs.\ 0.660), recovering $\sim$73\% of the accuracy lost to quantization.
110	The four non-spread architectures show minor average degradation (Yi $-$0.8, Llama $-$1.0, Mistral $-$0.5, Gemma-2 $+$0.1 pts); Llama is the most systematic, with 0 of 5 tasks showing positive change.
111	ARC-Challenge shows the largest per-task sensitivity across all models (Yi $-$3.2, Llama $-$2.7, Mistral $-$1.2, Gemma-2 $-$0.2 pts), consistent with multi-step reasoning where KV cache errors accumulate across longer inference chains.
112	Cross-dataset (Appendix~\ref{sec:cross_dataset}, ${>}96\%$ bit-assignment agreement across WikiText-2/C4) and long-context (Appendix~\ref{sec:long_context}, Qwen uniform $11.15\times$ bf16 at 8K vs.\ MCKP $1.23\times$) analyses confirm allocation robustness.

1	\section{Analysis}
2	\label{sec:analysis}
3	
4	\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
5	\label{sec:heterogeneity}
6	
7	The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
8	We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
9	High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.
10	
11	Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across seven models at $4\times$ compression.
12	The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.
13	
14	Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
15	Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.10 PPL, a 29.4\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp
16	
17	Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
18	Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 ($d_h(2){=}13.12$, second-ranked head: $0.55$, a $24\times$ gap; $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
19	Critically, L4H3's 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$, so upgrading it from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go---a ``spike'' pattern with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.
20	In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern enabling meaningful reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling
21	
22	Llama-3.1-8B has concentration $0.57$---comparable to Qwen's $0.61$---yet its spike pattern ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$), dominated by a single head (L2H5), yields allocation indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38), demonstrating that concentration alone is insufficient without spread structure. %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
23	Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.38$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.24$ and $0.23$), leaving no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.16 vs.\ $+$0.14 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline
24	
25	Pythia-1.4B extends the evaluation to MHA (1:1 ratio, 384 heads).
26	Low concentration ($0.24$) and $t_1/t_5{=}0.28$ place it in the flat category; constrained MCKP confirms this ($+$7.96 vs.\ uniform $+$7.80, $+$0.7\%). %exp_id=pythia14b_constrained_pipeline
27	
28	\paragraph{Scale-dependent concentration dilution.}
29	Qwen2.5-14B (GQA 5:1, 384 heads) provides a within-family comparison: $t_1/t_5$ is similar (0.57 vs.\ 0.68), but concentration drops from 0.61 (7B) to 0.33 (14B)---diluted by $3.4\times$ more heads into the flat regime.
30	Sensitivity is dominated by a single head (L0H5, $d_h(2){=}1.845$; second-ranked: $0.237$, a $7.8\times$ gap), but 384 heads dilute cumulative signal below the concentration threshold.
31	Concentration, not within-head structure, is thus the primary discriminator: the rule correctly identifies Qwen-7B as the single model$\times$scale combination where non-uniform allocation helps.

34	\centering
35	\small
36	\caption{Head sensitivity heterogeneity and constrained allocation benefit at $4\times$ compression. $t_1/t_5$: ratio of the most sensitive head's 2-bit distortion to the sum of the top-5\% heads' distortions (low${=}$spread, high${=}$spike). $^*$BOS-corrected.}
37	\label{tab:heterogeneity}
38	\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
39	\toprule
40	Model & GQA & Top-5\% & $t_1/t_5$ & $\Delta$ PPL & $\Delta$ PPL & Shape \\
41	 & Ratio & Conc. & & (Uniform) & (Ours) & \\
42	\midrule
43	Qwen2.5-7B & 7:1 & 0.61 & 0.57 & $+$5.64 & $+$1.10 & Spread \\
44	Qwen2.5-14B & 5:1 & 0.33 & 0.68 & $+$0.33 & $+$0.35 & Flat \\
45	Yi-1.5-9B & 8:1 & 0.71 & 0.90 & $+$0.20 & $+$0.20 & Spike \\

48	Gemma-2-9B$^*$ & 2:1 & 0.23 & 0.38 & $+$0.14 & $+$0.16 & Flat \\
49	Pythia-1.4B & 1:1 & 0.24 & 0.28 & $+$7.80 & $+$7.96 & Flat \\
50	\bottomrule
51	\end{tabular}
52	\end{table}
53	
54	The per-head heatmap (Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap}, Appendix~\ref{sec:heatmap_appendix}) confirms this visually: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero (spread); Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (64\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform (spike); Gemma-2 and Mistral show uniformly low distortion.
55	
56	\subsection{Empirical Decision Rule}
57	\label{sec:diagnostic}
58	
59	MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
60	This motivates a joint empirical decision rule for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile.
61	Given the profiling results from \S\ref{sec:profiling}, compute the top-5\% concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio, then select:
62	\begin{itemize}[nosep]
63	\item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform recommended. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): $-$29.4\% PPL.
64	\item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, concentration $\gtrsim 0.25$): use uniform. A dominant outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient cannot be exploited. Yi-1.5 (0.71, 0.90) and Llama (0.57, 0.85): no benefit.
65	\item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.25$, or remaining moderate-concentration models with $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): use uniform. Too little cumulative delta for meaningful reallocation. Mistral (0.24), Gemma-2 (0.23), Qwen-14B (0.33), and Pythia (0.24): no benefit or counterproductive.
66	\end{itemize}
67	
68	Both conditions are needed: Llama ($0.57$) and Yi-1.5 ($0.71$) both exceed the concentration threshold yet show no MCKP benefit; their spike shapes ($t_1/t_5 \geq 0.70$) correctly override.
69	A concentration-only rule would misclassify both as spread; $t_1/t_5$ is the critical second discriminator.
70	The rule correctly classifies all seven evaluated models (7/7), including the within-family scale contrast (Qwen-7B spread vs.\ 14B flat) and the MHA architecture (Pythia-1.4B flat).
71	Only Qwen-7B exhibits the spread pattern ($N{=}1$); the suggested thresholds should be treated as illustrative until confirmed on additional spread architectures.
72	The rule reuses profiling data already required by the solver and adds no overhead.
73	
74	Additional analyses---granularity tradeoff (Appendix~\ref{sec:granularity}), aggressive compression, profiling resolution and stability, per-layer optimality, and KV separation---are in Appendices~\ref{sec:granularity}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across seven models at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.10 PPL, a 29.4\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 ($d_h(2){=}13.12$, second-ranked head: $0.55$, a $24\times$ gap; $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$, so upgrading it from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go---a ``spike'' pattern with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.
In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern enabling meaningful reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

Llama-3.1-8B has concentration $0.57$---comparable to Qwen's $0.61$---yet its spike pattern ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$), dominated by a single head (L2H5), yields allocation indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38), demonstrating that concentration alone is insufficient without spread structure. %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.38$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.24$ and $0.23$), leaving no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.16 vs.\ $+$0.14 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

Pythia-1.4B extends the evaluation to MHA (1:1 ratio, 384 heads).
Low concentration ($0.24$) and $t_1/t_5{=}0.28$ place it in the flat category; constrained MCKP confirms this ($+$7.96 vs.\ uniform $+$7.80, $+$0.7\%). %exp_id=pythia14b_constrained_pipeline

\paragraph{Scale-dependent concentration dilution.}
Qwen2.5-14B (GQA 5:1, 384 heads) provides a within-family comparison: $t_1/t_5$ is similar (0.57 vs.\ 0.68), but concentration drops from 0.61 (7B) to 0.33 (14B)---diluted by $3.4\times$ more heads into the flat regime.
Sensitivity is dominated by a single head (L0H5, $d_h(2){=}1.845$; second-ranked: $0.237$, a $7.8\times$ gap), but 384 heads dilute cumulative signal below the concentration threshold.
Concentration, not within-head structure, is thus the primary discriminator: the rule correctly identifies Qwen-7B as the single model$\times$scale combination where non-uniform allocation helps.

\centering
\small
\caption{Head sensitivity heterogeneity and constrained allocation benefit at $4\times$ compression. $t_1/t_5$: ratio of the most sensitive head's 2-bit distortion to the sum of the top-5\% heads' distortions (low${=}$spread, high${=}$spike). $^*$BOS-corrected.}
\label{tab:heterogeneity}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Model & GQA & Top-5\% & $t_1/t_5$ & $\Delta$ PPL & $\Delta$ PPL & Shape \\

\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B & 7:1 & 0.61 & 0.57 & $+$5.64 & $+$1.10 & Spread \\
Qwen2.5-14B & 5:1 & 0.33 & 0.68 & $+$0.33 & $+$0.35 & Flat \\

Gemma-2-9B$^*$ & 2:1 & 0.23 & 0.38 & $+$0.14 & $+$0.16 & Flat \\
Pythia-1.4B & 1:1 & 0.24 & 0.28 & $+$7.80 & $+$7.96 & Flat \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The per-head heatmap (Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap}, Appendix~\ref{sec:heatmap_appendix}) confirms this visually: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero (spread); Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (64\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform (spike); Gemma-2 and Mistral show uniformly low distortion.

\subsection{Empirical Decision Rule}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint empirical decision rule for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile.
Given the profiling results from \S\ref{sec:profiling}, compute the top-5\% concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio, then select:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform recommended. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): $-$29.4\% PPL.
\item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, concentration $\gtrsim 0.25$): use uniform. A dominant outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient cannot be exploited. Yi-1.5 (0.71, 0.90) and Llama (0.57, 0.85): no benefit.
\item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.25$, or remaining moderate-concentration models with $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): use uniform. Too little cumulative delta for meaningful reallocation. Mistral (0.24), Gemma-2 (0.23), Qwen-14B (0.33), and Pythia (0.24): no benefit or counterproductive.
\end{itemize}

Both conditions are needed: Llama ($0.57$) and Yi-1.5 ($0.71$) both exceed the concentration threshold yet show no MCKP benefit; their spike shapes ($t_1/t_5 \geq 0.70$) correctly override.
A concentration-only rule would misclassify both as spread; $t_1/t_5$ is the critical second discriminator.
The rule correctly classifies all seven evaluated models (7/7), including the within-family scale contrast (Qwen-7B spread vs.\ 14B flat) and the MHA architecture (Pythia-1.4B flat).
Only Qwen-7B exhibits the spread pattern ($N{=}1$); the suggested thresholds should be treated as illustrative until confirmed on additional spread architectures.
The rule reuses profiling data already required by the solver and adds no overhead.

Additional analyses---granularity tradeoff (Appendix~\ref{sec:granularity}), aggressive compression, profiling resolution and stability, per-layer optimality, and KV separation---are in Appendices~\ref{sec:granularity}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding.
On Qwen2.5-7B, limiting 2-bit heads to $k{\leq}8$ reduces PPL from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 10.91 ($-$29.4\%) at $4\times$ compression, while making solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures.
Whether non-uniform allocation helps depends on the \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity---spread patterns (Qwen-7B, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$) yield large gains, while spike (Yi-1.5, Llama) and flat (Mistral, Gemma-2, Qwen-14B, Pythia) patterns show no benefit.
A joint empirical decision rule based on concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio correctly classifies all seven evaluated models (7/7), including a within-family scale contrast where Qwen-14B's spread dilutes into flat.
Extending to 70B+ models, production inference engines, and per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) are natural next steps.

\section*{Limitations}

Spread rests on $N{=}1$ (Qwen2.5-7B); the seven-model evaluation is directional, not robust. No real-kernel latency benchmarks; untested beyond 14B.

+\section{Granularity Tradeoff}
+\label{sec:granularity}
+
+Quantization budget can in principle be allocated at three granularities, each with a distinct cost--benefit profile.
+\emph{Layer-level} allocation (KVmix~\cite{li2025kvmix}, KVTuner~\cite{li2025kvtuner}) keeps the search space small ($L$ layers) but forces all heads in a layer to share one bitwidth.

+\emph{Token-level} allocation (ZipCache~\cite{he2024zipcache}, KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi}) is the finest grain available but introduces runtime overhead from online importance scoring.
+Importantly, per-head and per-token granularities are orthogonal: a head's bitwidth (static, determined offline) and a token's importance (dynamic, determined online) compose without conflict, so the two can be combined.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{KV Cache Quantization.}
Uniform-precision methods quantize the KV cache at a single bit-width across all heads, using techniques such as asymmetric per-channel/per-token schemes~\cite{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant}, quantization--serving co-design~\cite{lin2024qserve}, salient-token identification~\cite{he2024zipcache}, low-rank plus sparse correction~\cite{kang2024gear}, sliding-window adaptation~\cite{duanmu2024skvq}, rotation-based outlier smoothing for robust 2-bit~\cite{su2025rotatekv}, 2-bit with adaptive token retention~\cite{sharma2025minikv}, and adapter-based inter-layer prediction at 2--2.5 bits~\cite{shutova2025aquakv}.
We extend the design space to per-head non-uniform allocation over hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2,4,8,16\}$.
Our per-head bit-width allocation is orthogonal to per-channel quantization schemes such as KIVI: KIVI determines \emph{how} each head is quantized (asymmetric per-channel scaling), while our method determines \emph{at what precision} (bit-width selection across heads).
The two can be composed---a KIVI-quantized cache with per-head mixed precision---so our contribution is complementary, not competitive.

\paragraph{KV Cache Eviction.}
Complementary to quantization, eviction methods reduce cache size by discarding tokens---retaining heavy-hitters~\cite{zhang2023h2o}, per-head important tokens~\cite{li2024snapkv,ge2024fastgen}, persistent-importance tokens~\cite{liu2024scissorhands}, attention sinks~\cite{xiao2024streamingllm}, or progressively fewer tokens in deeper layers~\cite{yang2024pyramidinfer}.
Recent per-head eviction methods allocate non-uniform budgets across heads based on retrieval-vs-reasoning importance~\cite{fu2025headkv} or adaptive optimization extending SnapKV/PyramidKV~\cite{feng2025adakv}, confirming that head-level heterogeneity is exploitable for eviction; our work shows it is equally exploitable for quantization.


\paragraph{Mixed-Precision Quantization (Weights).}
Mixed-precision allocation has a long history at the weight level.
HAWQ~\cite{dong2019hawq} and HAWQ-V2~\cite{dong2020hawqv2} use second-order (Hessian-based) sensitivity to assign per-layer bit-widths, with V2 introducing block-wise trace-weighted scoring and Pareto-frontier selection; HAQ~\cite{wang2019haq} learns an allocation by reinforcement learning under hardware-aware latency/energy constraints.
These methods operate on weights, where per-layer distortions are approximately additive and sensitivity varies smoothly across layers.
KV cache quantization presents a qualitatively different challenge: 2-bit head distortions compound super-additively through the residual stream (\S\ref{sec:compounding}), a phenomenon absent in weight quantization where each layer's parameters are independently quantized.
Our primary contribution is not the allocation algorithm itself---any MCKP or greedy solver suffices---but the diagnosis and fix of this compounding effect via cardinality constraints, and the characterization of when non-uniform allocation is beneficial (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).

\paragraph{Mixed-Precision Rate-Distortion Allocation.}
RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} formulates per-head bit-width selection as an MCKP and proves greedy optimality for consecutive bit-widths $\{2,\ldots,6\}$ via the polymatroid structure, which relies on the assumption that per-head distortions decompose additively into the global objective---valid when adjacent bit-widths differ by a single bit so that quantization noise stays in the small-perturbation regime.
On hardware-aligned $\{2,4,8,16\}$, the 4$\times$ gap between 2-bit and 4-bit drives 2-bit distortion to compound super-additively, breaking the polymatroid structure and the additivity assumption with it.
Concretely, running RateQuant's greedy algorithm (Algorithm~1) directly on $\{2,4,8,16\}$ yields 32.45 PPL on Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression---catastrophically worse than uniform 4-bit (15.45)---whereas our cardinality constraint on simultaneously active 2-bit heads recovers 10.91 PPL at the same average bit-width.
The constraint is the minimal fix that restores the additive regime in which RateQuant's polymatroid argument applies.
Related mixed-precision KV-cache work operates at coarser granularity---layer-level via gradient-based sensitivity~\cite{li2025kvmix} or Pareto search over hardware-friendly precision pairs~\cite{li2025kvtuner}, block-level via progressive decoding-step quantization for long-CoT reasoning~\cite{liu2025pmkvq}, channel-level via dynamic precision boost on sensitive Key channels~\cite{xia2025kitty}, token-level via a learned on-device controller~\cite{haeriboroujeni2026dontwaste}, memory-budget-level~\cite{lei2026arkv}---at the weight level~\cite{kim2024squeezellm}, or dynamically at inference time~\cite{zhang2025mixkvq}; our allocation is static and per-head.

\paragraph{Attention Head Analysis.}
Prior work studies head redundancy and pruning~\cite{voita2019analyzing,michel2019sixteen}, focusing on which heads can be removed entirely.
Our analysis asks a different question: which heads are sensitive to \emph{quantization}, and how heterogeneous that sensitivity is across architectures---a property that determines whether non-uniform allocation is beneficial (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).

Unconstrained failure severity tracks heterogeneity shape: \emph{catastrophic} on Qwen-7B ($3.3\times$ bf16, 60\% heads at 2-bit), \emph{severe} on Pythia ($1.9\times$), \emph{moderate} on Gemma-2 ($1.47\times$), and \emph{mild} on remaining models (${\sim}1.07$--$1.12\times$) including Qwen-14B ($1.12\times$, 20\% 2-bit)---the within-family contrast directly reflects shape (spread vs.\ flat).
See Appendix~\ref{sec:allocation_appendix} (allocation visualization) and Appendix~\ref{sec:budget_sweep} (budget sweep) for additional detail.

MCKP consistently outperforms random L0-constrained allocation and naive positional baselines across all three tested models (median gap 5--16\%; Table~\ref{tab:heuristic} in Appendix~\ref{sec:heuristic_appendix}).

\paragraph{Comparison with KIVI.}
KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi} uses asymmetric per-channel quantization with per-token scaling, applied uniformly across all heads.
At 4-bit ($r{=}0$), KIVI achieves near-lossless PPL (9.91 on Qwen, 8.14 on Llama vs.\ 9.81/8.09 bf16), while our symmetric scheme yields 15.45 and 8.47---a gap from the quantization method, not allocation.
Within the symmetric scheme, constrained MCKP reduces Qwen from 15.45 to 10.91 ($-$4.54 PPL) by reallocating bits across heads; on Llama (spike), the gain is negligible ($-$0.02).
The two approaches are orthogonal and composable: KIVI selects the per-channel scheme, our method selects the per-head bit-width.
However, composability does not imply additive benefit: on Qwen, KIVI+MCKP achieves 9.90 PPL---identical to KIVI alone (9.90; MCKP alone: 10.89), as the per-channel method subsumes the head-level reallocation signal.
Per-head allocation provides independent value in symmetric-only deployment environments---common in hardware accelerators that lack per-channel asymmetric support---where it is the sole degree of freedom for exploiting sensitivity heterogeneity.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache is a natural strategy for reducing memory during LLM inference: assign fewer bits to insensitive heads and more bits to sensitive ones, achieving lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width.
Recent work on KV cache quantization explores both uniform schemes~\cite{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant,lin2024qserve,he2024zipcache} and token-level mixed-precision approaches~\cite{ge2024fastgen,lei2026arkv}, while complementary methods reduce cache size through eviction~\cite{zhang2023h2o,li2024snapkv}.
RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} formalizes per-head allocation as a rate-distortion optimization and shows that greedy allocation is optimal when bit-widths are consecutive integers $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, exploiting the polymatroid structure of the feasible set (their Proposition~6).

In practice, hardware-efficient inference requires bit-widths drawn from $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$---the formats natively supported by modern accelerators.
On this non-consecutive set, the polymatroid structure breaks down, and greedy is no longer provably optimal.
One might expect that exact MCKP solvers would fill this gap.
They do not.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, unconstrained greedy achieves 32.45 PPL and unconstrained MCKP achieves 36.92---both \emph{far worse} than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
The optimization does not merely underperform; it fails catastrophically.

The root cause is not solver suboptimality but a violation of the additive distortion assumption.
Both solvers assign 68--75 of 112 KV heads to 2-bit, where per-head quantization errors compound through the residual stream.
The additive model predicts $\sim$11 PPL; the actual PPL is $3$--$4\times$ higher, because 2-bit distortions are orders of magnitude larger than 4-bit and compound super-linearly when many heads are quantized simultaneously.

This observation points to a minimal intervention: cap the number of 2-bit assignments.
We add a single cardinality constraint $\sum_h \mathbb{1}[b_h{=}2] \leq k$ to the standard MCKP formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}).
On Qwen2.5-7B, setting $k{=}8$ (7\% of heads) yields 10.91 PPL---a 29.4\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint works by forcing the solver to use 2-bit only on the least-sensitive heads, while redistributing the freed budget to protect sensitive heads at 8-bit or 16-bit.
This is not a heuristic patch: the constraint directly addresses the identified failure mode and is compatible with any solver.
The constraint is beneficial even on flat-distribution architectures: on Gemma-2-9B, unconstrained MCKP assigns 31.5\% of heads to 2-bit, producing a moderate $1.47\times$ degradation; the constraint reduces this to within 0.5\% of uniform.

A surprising consequence is that the cardinality constraint renders solver choice irrelevant.
Constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures (112/112 heads on Qwen, 256/256 on Llama, 255/256 on Mistral), enabling practitioners to use the simpler $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm.
A per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality: the maximum gap is 0.02 PPL, 0.4\% of the total improvement (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

However, non-uniform allocation does not help universally.
On the remaining six models---including Qwen2.5-14B, where the $3.4\times$ increase in head count dilutes spread into flat---constrained MCKP provides no meaningful improvement.
The difference traces to the \emph{distribution shape} of head sensitivity, not GQA ratio or model scale alone: Qwen-7B's Layer-0 heads form a cluster of high sensitivity across multiple bitwidths (``spread''); Yi-1.5 and Llama have dominant outliers (``spike''); Gemma-2, Mistral, Qwen-14B, and Pythia show near-uniform or diluted sensitivity (``flat'').

This motivates a question prior work does not address: \emph{when} should a practitioner use per-head mixed-precision quantization?
We propose a joint empirical decision rule based on concentration and distribution shape (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}) that correctly classifies all seven evaluated models (7/7), including a within-family scale contrast.
Yi-1.5 is a critical test: its concentration ($0.71$) exceeds Qwen-7B's, but its single-outlier spike has no cross-bitwidth gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item We identify 2-bit distortion compounding as the cause of catastrophic failure in unconstrained per-head KV cache quantization on hardware-aligned bit-widths, and show that a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix, reducing Qwen2.5-7B PPL from 32--37 (unconstrained) to 10.91 (constrained) at $4\times$ compression (\S\ref{sec:compounding}, \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\item We demonstrate that the cardinality constraint serves three roles: preventing catastrophic failure on spread architectures (Qwen: 32.45$\to$10.91), preventing moderate over-allocation on flat architectures (Gemma-2: 8.85$\to$within 0.5\% of uniform), and rendering solver choice irrelevant---constrained greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all tested architectures (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

\item We propose a joint empirical decision rule combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly classifies all seven evaluated models (7/7), including a within-family scale contrast (Qwen-7B spread vs.\ 14B flat). Yi-1.5-9B serves as a critical test: its concentration exceeds Qwen-7B's, yet its single-outlier spike pattern means MCKP provides no benefit over uniform (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
\end{enumerate}
